results.title: Intraclass correlation coefficients for weight loss cluster randomized trials in primary care: The PROPEL trial
results.content: The aim of this study was to compute intra-class correlations (ICCs) for weight-related and patient-reported outcomes in a cluster randomized clinical trial (cRCT) for weight loss. The proper design of a cRCT requires estimates of the ICC, which are often obtained from published studies.11 Indeed, the CONSORT extension to cRCTs calls for reporting the ICC for each primary outcome.12 Estimates of ICCs have been published for a variety of outcomes and for different settings (communities, schools, worksites, and medical clinics).7 Primary care remains the cornerstone of medical care in the United States; thus, primary care clinics are an important setting for pragmatic trials. ICCs have been reported for primary care trials for binary and continuous clinical outcomes and process of care measures.13–17 Despite using data from cRCTs (longitudinal designs), four of these studies used baseline data only to compute the ICCs.13–15,17 This approach limits the usefulness of the computed ICCs in informing sample size estimates for interventions where the outcomes are expressed as changes from baseline (e.g., changes in risk factors), or follow-up values (sometimes adjusted for baseline values). Adams and colleagues re-analyzed data from 31 cluster-based studies in primary care to compute ICCs for multiple outcomes.18 Most of the data were cross-sectional, with the exception of baseline and follow-up data from 12 studies; however, ICCs were not computed for changes over time, nor for specific variables.18 Therefore, there is a need to report ICCs based on longitudinal analyses of cRCTs to properly estimate sample sizes for future studies. However, these comparisons of cross-sectional results highlight the variability in ICCs derived in different contexts, and support the contention that the design of future studies should be based on data from similar populations (i.e., sex, age, race, socioeconomic status, etc.) in similar contexts (i.e., primary care, specialty clinics, community health centers, etc.). * In order to account for the clustering of patients within groups, estimates of intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) are often used to inform sample size requirements when designing cluster-randomized trials. * This study extends the results of previous studies by presenting ICCs for several weight-related outcomes, cardiometabolic risk factors, and patient-reported outcomes derived from a large cluster-randomized weight loss trial conducted in primary care.

results.title: Intraclass correlation coefficients for cluster randomized trials in care pathways and usual care: hospital treatment for heart failure - PMC
results.content: # Intraclass correlation coefficients for cluster randomized trials in care pathways and usual care: hospital treatment for heart failure. In order to perform a well-designed cluster randomized trial to demonstrate the effectiveness of Usual care (UC) and CP in heart failure treatment, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) should be available before conducting a trial to estimate the required sample size. This study reports ICCs for both demographical and outcome variables from cluster randomized trials of heart failure patients in UC and care pathways. Reported values of ICCs from present care pathway trial and UC results for some common outcomes will be helpful for estimating sample size in future clustered randomized heart failure trials, in particular for the evaluation of care pathways. The present study reports ICCs for both demographical and outcome variables from cluster randomized trials of heart failure patients in the setting of usual care (UC) and care pathways (CP). Reported values of ICCs obtained from the UC and care pathway trials for some common outcomes would be useful to estimate sample size in future CP trials. Tables 3 and 4 provide estimates of intraclass correlation coefficients, 95% confidence intervals and design effects for baseline characteristics for each cluster and outcomes of the clustered sample selected from 14 hospitals (7 CP, 7 UC). In the present study, ICCs and their associated 95% confidence intervals were calculated for clinical and patient-related outcome variables based on the results of an Italian multi-center cluster randomized trial of heart failure. Since a CRT design was used in the current study, our results may be helpful for estimating the effect size in future randomized trials of in-hospital treatment of heart failure. In the present study, ICCs for multiple outcomes were reported with the aim to help facilitate the design process of future cluster randomized trials, particularly for therapeutic interventions for hospitalized heart failure patients. A cluster randomized controlled trial of a clinical pathway for hospital treatment of heart failure: study design and population.
